A major difference between survival data and most standard regression datasets is that there is a term called right censoring. Under right censoring, the event has not been observed by the end of the available follow-up period. For example, a patient may remain alive until the end of the study, meaning that the exact event time is unknown, although it is known that the patient remained event-free throughout the observed follow-up period. As a result, the time that is observed is the minimum between the true times and the censoring time. Specifically, survival methods are meant to hold onto the information found in such observations and not to take them merely as missing outcomes \cite{ref1}, \cite{ref3}.

Huang et al. \cite{ref1} present a scoping review of machine learning works on predicting survival using real world healthcare data. This gives an idea of the diversity of the literature in the disease, sample size, algorithms, validation and metrics. The synthesis indicated that random survival forests and neural networks are widely used. This however was not consistently validated. The current paper offers valuable information on the process of generating applied evidence and the reasons why the outcomes might not be generalizable in accordance to the studies. However, the evidence is limited as there was a small amount of evidence. It cannot be assumed that machine learning will always outperform Cox regression due to the varied applications. The authors emphasize that the selection of a model is based on the features of the data and validation. This thus justifies the incorporation of flexible models to compare. Nevertheless, one cannot presume that flexible models will necessarily work better. The necessity of this thesis has been to say that the outputs of this experiment are available in only a few pairs of model-cohorts.

original_citation_contexts.paragraph: Survival analysis deals with time to event outcomes, unlike a standard classification/regression problem, it accounts for both the time to the occurrence of an event and censored data (right). In healthcare, events may include death, recurrence, progression, treatment failure and re-admission. The survival literature has recently reviewed how these techniques have been extended to machine learning prediction \cite{ref1} \cite{ref2}.

Conventional classification and regression methods are inadequate for many clinical time-to-event problems because they do not naturally account for censoring and the timing of events. A classification model is capable of estimating whether or not an event happens in a known time frame, but is not naturally descriptive of the entire distribution of the time of the event. Likewise, Standard regression generally assumes that the outcome is observed for each individual and does not explicitly model right-censored event times \cite{ref2}, \cite{ref4}. This is a critical difference in the context of healthcare since two patients can end up having the same clinical outcome but with significantly different timeframes to such outcome.

Survival analysis is widely used in healthcare because many clinically important outcomes are inherently time-dependent. Survival prediction can be applied to overall mortality, disease recurrence, disease progression, treatment outcomes, and patient prognosis. In cancer biology, overall survival and progression-free survival are often employed to measure survival time and disease progression in the patient. Recent surveys of machine-learning survival models in clinical data reveal that oncology is one of the most glaring fields of application, and survival models are often applied to forecast the prognosis and clinical events of disease \cite{ref2}.

The prediction of survival can also be used to analyze recurrence and progress of the disease. Instead of categorizing patients as either likely or unlikely to recur, a survival model is able to attempt to determine the likelihood of patients spending a series of future time points without recurrence. This gives data, which might be applicable in deciding on the intensity of follow-up and monitoring needs. On the same note, estimates of mortality risk can be done using survival methods and taking into consideration variations in patient characteristics and follow-up time \cite{ref2}, \cite{ref5}.

The growing availability of electronic health records, genomic data, and other clinical data sources has created further opportunities for survival prediction. Machine-learning techniques can accommodate complex predictor structures and identify nonlinear relationships that may be difficult to capture using conventional linear predictors. A scoping review of recent real-world healthcare published papers in 2023 reported that time-to-event prediction based on random survival forests and neural networks is becoming highly popular and that many involve prognosis and clinical event predictions \cite{ref2}.

The Cox proportional-hazards model then offered a model to correlate individual covariates with the risk of occurrence of an event. Its semi-parametric formulation permits the covariate effects to be estimated without any specific parametric distribution of the baseline hazard. As a result, Cox regression has been a critical reference point in clinical survival prediction, and will still be a relatively interpretable reference point to the newer methods \cite{ref2}, \cite{ref6}.

The advent of machine-learning survival models added more flexibility in modeling nonlinear relationships and interactions. Random survival forests, such as those, are an extension of tree-based ensemble learning to censored time-to-event observations. These methods have the capability of capturing structures that might be challenging to represent with a standard linear predictor \cite{ref2}.

original_citation_contexts.paragraph: Conventional classification and regression methods are inadequate for many clinical time-to-event problems because they do not naturally account for censoring and the timing of events. A classification model is capable of estimating whether or not an event happens in a known time frame, but is not naturally descriptive of the entire distribution of the time of the event. Likewise, Standard regression generally assumes that the outcome is observed for each individual and does not explicitly model right-censored event times \cite{ref2}, \cite{ref4}. This is a critical difference in the context of healthcare since two patients can end up having the same clinical outcome but with significantly different timeframes to such outcome.

A deep learning method named DeepSurv was proposed for personalized survival prediction and treatment recommendation \cite{ref4}. Although the model-based prediction can help in prognosis, causal treatment effects can only be identified with a specific design and assumptions.

There have been many proposed deep learning survival models. These utilise neural networks to represent relationships between covariates and outcome. DeepSurv was the first model to incorporate a Cox regression loss function \cite{ref4}. A review of neural networks for survival analysis can be found in \cite{ref5}. Continuous and discrete time models are compared in \cite{ref21}.

Katzman et al. \cite{ref4} introduce DeepSurv, a feedforward neural network to replace the linear predictor in the Cox model with a non-linear risk function. Experiments are presented demonstrating how patient covariates and treatment can be used to assess individualised risk and treatment recommendations. This provides added flexibility by increasing the range of the predictor function. Interactions can be modelled using neural networks that would have to be manually specified in a standard Cox model. However, it is still based on the PH assumption and is still framed around the partial likelihood. The hazard ratio is not time dependent as it is using a flexible network. Causal assumptions must also be made to recommend treatment.

The third stage of the process broke down the modelling into a baseline and Bayesian approach. CoxPH, RSF and DeepSurv were applied to create a reference survival model. DeepSurv is a neural network version of the Cox proportional hazards predictor \cite{ref4}. Studies have shown that the relative performance can vary between different datasets \cite{ref33}, \cite{ref38}. Hence, multiple comparison families should be used.

The DeepSurv model used had 2 hidden layers (32, 16). The model had a dropout of 0.10, Adam optimizer with learning rate 0.001, L2 weight decay of 0.0001 and was trained using full batch training with early stopping (patience 20, max 150 epochs). The model had 3-fold cross-validation within the inner training fold to find the best architecture. The model had either 2 hidden layers (32, 16) or (64, 32) with a dropout of 0 or 0.10. The best model was found to be (32, 16) with a dropout of 0.10. This was trained for 132 epochs. The final model was refitted using the outer training fold. The log risk score was combined with the Breslow baseline from the training fold to predict the survival probabilities of the holdouts. DeepSurv allows for non-linear predictor effects but still uses the Cox proportional hazards objective function \cite{ref4}.

Katzman et al. have shown that DeepSurv performs well on simulated and clinical survival data. It can be seen as a neural version of the Cox survival model for personal risk prediction \cite{ref4}. The model provides a very different computational reference but still has a familiar survival risk prediction structure.The three baselines are used jointly to denote conventional statistical modelling (CoxPH), the nonlinear ensemble learning (RSF), and neural survival modelling (DeepSurv). This combination offers a significant methodological reference to assess the Bayesian piecewise-exponential proportional-hazards models.

original_citation_contexts.paragraph: Bayesian survival modelling represents another methodological development, providing posterior distributions rather than only point estimates. Bayesian approaches provide a kind of probability distribution of unknown parameters and combine prior knowledge with observed data to get the posterior distributions. Survival methods based on Bayesian methods can thus offer a clear description of parameter uncertainty as well as allow other prior structures to be explored. Bayesian variable-selection studies have shown that prior distributions can be used to control the choice of coefficients and shrinkage in censored survival data, especially in high-dimensional clinical and genomic settings \cite{ref8}.

The growing use of Bayesian methods for survival prediction raises an important methodological question concerning the specification of regression-coefficient priors. In Bayesian inference, prior distributions represent assumptions about plausible parameter values before the observed data are incorporated. The posterior distribution is then obtained by combining the prior distribution with the likelihood of the observed data. Therefore, the chosen prior may affect the posterior coefficient estimates, the uncertainty and predictive behaviour, especially when the information in the data is restricted \cite{ref8}.

This issue is particularly important for survival datasets because the information available for estimating covariate effects depends not only on sample size but also on the number of observed events and the extent of censoring. Moreover, clinical datasets can also have correlated predictors, and it can be hard to tell whether a closely related variable is an independent one. It has been demonstrated that Bayesian variable-selection studies can regularise coefficients with prior structures to solve variable-selection issues in censored survival data \cite{ref8}.

original_citation_contexts.paragraph: In and Lee \cite{ref14} offer a good background to time-to-event data, the structure of the data, the estimation of Kaplan-Meier, a log-rank test and Cox regression. The tutorial gives a good explanation of what is being estimated and the importance of the risk sets. The article clarifies core survival-analysis procedures but does not provide comparative evidence on predictive performance or define the endpoint and censoring process for this study. It therefore serves as methodological background rather than direct evidence for model selection. The thesis presents valuable methodological information to help justify why it is significant to have censored individuals on the time that they were observed. It also gives a clear picture on the distinction between the descriptive survival curves and predictive models. General explanations presented in this paper should be backed by empirical, methodological understanding to realize how the assumptions are broken and the usefulness of the predictions.

Perera and Dwivedi \cite{ref15} give a review of the statistical choices done in designing and analysing survival studies. This thesis provides a greater insight into why certain analyses are performed, helping to link the analysis to the study objectives. It also underscores the problem of inconsistency in methodologies that may lead to a problem in oncology. This thesis comes in handy in giving background to how the data would be prepared and the significance of the number of events, censoring and the definitions of predictors. The recommendations offered are however very general and could be applicable in a range of studies. It does not make a direct comparison of the existing survival learning techniques. Part of the recommendations would be general and hence they could not be applied in identifying the best chance or validation design of GBSG2, METABRIC and WHAS500. This, together with In and Lee \cite{ref14}, demonstrates the necessity of basic notions to be able to do a critical review. This study provides time and event variables according to each cohort and indicates that there is a restriction to the extent that can be assessed with the help of the holdout data.

original_citation_contexts.paragraph: Jachno, Heritier and Wolfe \cite{ref17} present a literature review of how the designs and analysis of randomised trials consider the non-constant hazard rates and non-proportional hazards. This is an important consideration as the hazard ratio may hide any time varying effects. This thesis will give an insight on how the design of a study can be influenced by the non-proportional hazards. The evidence presented, however, is mostly founded on randomised trials and treatment effects. The fact that there is no evidence to indicate that the data has non-proportional hazards implies that it cannot be used to examine Bayesian priors or predictive methods of machine learning. This therefore highlights the need to consider the assumptions and provide caveats. CoxPH is a reference model that is included in this thesis. But proportional covariate hazards is also assumed in the Bayesian piecewise exponential model. The problem of time varying covariates cannot be overcome by allowing the baseline hazard to be interval varying.

original_citation_contexts.paragraph: There have been many proposed deep learning survival models. These utilise neural networks to represent relationships between covariates and outcome. DeepSurv was the first model to incorporate a Cox regression loss function \cite{ref4}. A review of neural networks for survival analysis can be found in \cite{ref5}. Continuous and discrete time models are compared in \cite{ref21}.

Kvamme and Borgan \cite{ref21} compare the use of neural networks for continuous and discrete time survival prediction. This demonstrates how different likelihoods can be used with neural networks. Discretisation requires decisions to be made around the time grid. This is important to note as discretisation can sometimes be seen as a convenience. The boundaries of the interval will impact how the target is represented and how the model will predict. The empirical comparisons show how the performance of the methods will depend on the data and method used. The results from these datasets and implementations do not show that continuous or discrete methods will always outperform each other. The current thesis uses DeepSurv, which retains the Cox objective, and a Bayesian piecewise exponential model, which represents the baseline rates with intervals. This article helps to justify the choices made and shows how different likelihoods can be used. It is useful to note how the intervals were constructed, and that they were only derived during training.

original_citation_contexts.paragraph: Alvares et al. \cite{ref22} provide a tutorial review of Bayesian survival models using BUGS. This includes proportional hazards, accelerated failure time, cure, competing risk, multistate, frailty and joint models. The range of models is a key strength of this paper. It shows how Bayesian inference can be used to analyse a variety of event structures, and how the choice of likelihood and baseline depends on the research question. This paper provides practical advice on how to implement these models. However, as it is a tutorial review, it does not rank the methods under the same dataset. There is no controlled comparison between different priors on the coefficients. The examples cannot be assumed to provide evidence that any Bayesian model will be more accurate or interpretable than a frequentist approach. This paper provides justification for the methodology used in this thesis. It helps to narrow down the contribution of this study, as it is not looking to create a new Bayesian survival model. original_citation_contexts.paragraph: Park et al. \cite{ref26} review performance measures of traditional and new time-to-event prediction models. This gives a general idea of how to analyze models using varying properties. This gives a sound basis on which to comprehend how to assess ranking and correctness of probabilities. Nevertheless, it is not a new experiment, and is presented in a simple to follow format. Its broad-range makes it impossible to give particular suggestions on the most appropriate metric to be used. It also fails to consider the effects of a given censoring distribution on the evaluation. As noted in this thesis, the evaluation is based on the output of the model. In case a risk score is given, it can not be understood as the absolute likelihood of survival without additional information of the model. Thus, C-index and time dependent AUC have been used along with IPCW Brier and calibration in this analysis. This is because a high ranking does not ensure correct predictions. The conclusions are therefore specific to the cohorts and horizons.

Reproducibility was an important part of the computational analysis. A fixed random seed was used (260817). All parameters were specified for the models, priors, MCMC settings, diagnostics and what was being evaluated. The Bayesian models had 2000 warmup iterations and 2000 posterior samples were drawn. The target acceptance probabilities were specified per model. For the Normal and Spike-and-Slab models the target acceptance probabilities were 0.95. For the Horseshoe model the target acceptance probabilities were 0.99. The Normal, Horseshoe, and Spike-and-Slab model settings were recorded explicitly to support reproducibility.. This reduces the chance that differences in results are not due to changes in the calculations. Reproducible Bayesian workflows focus on specifying the computational details, diagnostics and re-validating model assumptions \cite{ref26}, \cite{ref35}, \cite{ref36}, \cite{ref37}.

This renders it a handy ranking metric. It however, fails to tell how similar the predicted probabilities are to the actual ones. This is especially pertinent to this thesis because it emphasizes the fact that the C-index cannot be viewed as a wholesome measure of the quality of a model. It also gives details on the process of the selection of models using this measure. This may be problematic in overfitting. A single concordance estimator cannot be used to completely remove any dependencies on the censoring patterns and support for follow-up. Thus C-index has been employed along with probability measures. The holdout fold is particularly described. The assumption of small differences in the C-index should not be that a model is clinically superior. Or that it can be rated among various cohorts.

original_citation_contexts.paragraph: The validation strategy was designed to avoid overfitting and to ensure the 3 healthcare cohorts had the time-to-event structure. Censoring, discrimination, prediction error and calibration need to be considered when predicting survival. Therefore, the evaluation strategy didn't rely on a single measure of performance. A review of methods of evaluating survival prediction highlights that discrimination, calibration and prediction error complement each other \cite{ref29}.

Three different survival model families were selected to compare with the Bayesian survival models. Cox proportional hazards (CoxPH), Random Survival Forest (RSF) and DeepSurv were implemented. This was done to provide different reference models. The performance of these models can be compared to each other based on the amount of events, censoring, structure of predictors, linearity, interactions and evaluation metrics. This can be done using comparative survival analysis \cite{ref29}.

Recent simulations have shown that neither model is always better. CoxPH can provide as strong performance in the presence of linear effects and little information on the event. RSF can benefit from situations with non-linearities and interactions \cite{ref29}.

The predictive evaluation model was created to see how well the model discriminates and predicts accurately the censored time-to-event results. Survival prediction is the prediction of the likelihood of a certain event happening and at what time. Thus, there is no single measure that can be applied to adequately describe the model performance. Contemporary methodological literature recommends discrimination, prediction error and calibration to be taken into account \cite{ref29}, \cite{ref43}. C-index informs us on the extent to which the model is able to rank patients based on the relative risk of events. Brier score informs us of the extent to which the forecasted survival is not similar to the actual. Time-dependent AUC informs us on how the model can differentiate at a certain follow-up time. The agreement between the predicted and observed probability of an event is measured by calibration \cite{ref43}, \cite{ref44}.

original_citation_contexts.paragraph: Krzyziński et al. \cite{ref30} propose SurvSHAP(t), an extension to Shapley values for time dependent survival model outputs. This addresses a real limitation of static feature importance. The predictor can impact survival predictions differently at different follow-up times. This can be used to describe how the output of the model changes across the survival curve. This is useful for black box models. However, this is only providing an explanation of how the fitted model arrived at the prediction. It does not provide evidence of etiological effects, posterior uncertainty or causal influences. The results will depend on the background data chosen and specific survival output. This is important to note as the main explanations in this thesis focus on posterior coefficient and hazard ratio summaries. This article provides justification for discussing time dependence and model specific explanations. It prevents confusion between posterior probabilities and local feature attributions. It also reinforces that explainability is not a replacement for calibration, validation and appropriate model diagnostics. The interpretation chosen in this thesis is based on the posterior draws that passed the stated diagnostics.

The three different Bayesian families are used for a variety of different methods. The Normal distribution is a fairly standard choice for continuous shrinkage. The Horseshoe distribution is a global-local shrinkage method. This has the capability to robustly shrink down the weak signals but keep the relatively robust effects unconstrained. This has been analysed in both regression and survival scenarios within Bayesian models where there can be many predictors with a small signal \cite{ref30}. The Spike-and-Slab distribution is another method to encourage sparsity in the model. In recent survival studies the spike-and-slab Cox models have been looked at specifically and shown to be used to detect sparse covariates \cite{ref34}.

The random survival forest provides a nonlinear comparator for CoxPH and the Bayesian proportional-hazards models. Its results help assess whether the additional Bayesian structure is associated with improved predictive performance in these cohorts. RSF has been used in high dimensional censored survival data \cite{ref30}.

It is a predetermined out of sample fold. The model metrics were not statistically analyzed. Cohort differences were observed to be descriptive. This prevents overstating slight numerical variations to indicate that generalized models are better. Published comparisons of survival models have pointed out that the discrimination and prediction error measures can tend to favour various models based on the structure and complexity of the cohort \cite{ref30}, \cite{ref48}, \cite{ref51}.

original_citation_contexts.paragraph: Alvares et al. \cite{ref90} provide a review on Bayesian survival analysis using Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation. This is a deterministic approximation for latent Gaussian models. This article demonstrates how a variety of survival structures can be represented for approximate Bayesian inference. It also highlights the computational benefits of using this method over sampling. This is useful to note as this thesis uses NUTS for MCMC inference. This shows that there is no single inference algorithm that must be used for Bayesian modelling. INLA can provide faster results for certain latent Gaussian models, but depends on how the model is represented, how accurate the approximation is and how it is implemented in software. This is not a plug-and-play method for all custom likelihoods and priors. The range of models covered do not directly compare INLA to NUTS under the piecewise exponential priors used in this project. This is therefore only relevant from a conceptual standpoint. The methods used in this thesis retain MCMC, and provide diagnostics.

This chapter has reported the results of three healthcare survival cohorts with differing event patterns and survival structures. The baseline models had varied results across the cohorts with no particular modelling method dominating the datasets. Eight Bayesian models were chosen to be fitted in the diagnostics framework. The GBSG2/Horseshoe was excluded due to not being able to recover diagnostics. There was a fixed final predictive evaluation with seven canonical pairs of cohort models. Also explained using hazard ratios, credible intervals and directional probabilities, the Bayesian posterior values also gave explainability at a coefficient level. None of the models or precedents were found to be the most effective with all indicators and groups \cite{ref90}.

Eq10 places the point-mass/gamma mixture on the spatial decay parameter gamma_k to distinguish spatially static from spatially varying effects. This mixture is not a spike-and-slab prior directly on the coefficient beta_k.
references.computation_distinction: Section4.1pp9–10first estimates site-specific partial-likelihood coefficients and covariance matrices, then approximates those estimates by a normal sampling model for second-stage hierarchical inference. It does not jointly fit a piecewise-exponential baseline and coefficients from raw survival observations.
